newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia runs out of cash to intensify drug war.
newsitem.headline: Colombia runs out of cash to intensify drug war.

text.p: Colombia is unable to step up its war on illegal drug crops because it cannot afford an expensive U.S.-made herbicide, outgoing Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra said in a newspaper interview on Monday.
Esguerra, who will become Colombia's ambassador to Washington, welcomed U.S. anti-narcotics aid, but said it was insufficient to confront the power of the drug cartels.

Colombia had hoped to begin widescale fumigation of coca leaf and opium poppy plantations with the herbicide Imazapyr, replacing glyphosate, a spray that has proven to be largely ineffective in wet and windy conditions.

"The National Anti-Drug Council approved the use of Imazapyr and the purchase of the necessary quantities from the (U.S) manufacturer. But there have been problems over the cost," Esguerra told the respected daily El Espectador.
He said the price difference was "considerable."

Last year, Colombia slightly exceeded the targets set in its U.S.-backed drug crop eradication programme and fumigated more than 44,500 acres (18,000 hectares) of coca leaf, the raw material for cocaine, and about 14,000 acres (6,500 hectares) of opium poppy, used for heroin production.
Colombia spent $985 million in its fight against drug production and trafficking while U.S. aid amounted to about $40 million.

"Any form of collaboration is welcome but if you ask me if (the U.S. contribution) is enough, then no it isn't. We're fighting such a rich, powerful enemy that no contribution will ever be enough," Esguerra said.
Imazapyr can be used in all weather conditions and comes in a granular form, allowing crop-dusting planes to fly higher and avoid the risk of attacks by armed gangs that protect the plantations.
Esguerra's first task when he arrives in Washington will be to convince the Clinton administration to reverse its decision, announced last March, to decertify Colombia as an ally in the drug war.

Colombia's drug cartels are still believed to supply 80 percent of the world's cocaine and edged out Southeast Asian drug traffickers to become the No.1 supplier of high grade heroin to the United States.
